2158.t: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew מִרְיָם (miryɔm)bor. Aramaic מריםbor.

2148.t: From Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (yōḥɔnɔn), the masculine form of יוֹחָנָה (yōḥānā), whence also Ἰωάννα (Ĭōắnnā).

2121.t: Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰn̥gʰ-ú-s, zero-grade u-stem of *dʰengʰ- (“to go quickly”), based on the comparison with Lithuanian déngti (“to run, hurry”) (see there for more potential cognates), though Fraenkel has disputed the connection.

2136.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hā́ls, from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l (“salt”). Cognates include Sanskrit सलिल (salila), Old Armenian աղ (ał), Latin sāl, and Old English sealt (English salt).

2151.t: Genitive singular of ὁμός (homós, “same”), used adverbially.

2159.t: From Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠Pārsa⁠/) + -ις (-ĭs, feminine suffix).

2126.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰugā́, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰugéh₂. Equivalent to φεύγω (pheúgō, “flee”) + -η (-ē, action noun suffix).

2101.t: Already in Late Mycenaean Greek (Ta-716 from Pylos), attested in the dual 𐀥𐀯𐀟𐀁 (qi-si-pe-e, “two swords”) (mostly ideographically as 𐃉).

2169.t: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”), with δύο (dŭ́o) coming from the indeclinable variant *d(u)wó.

2177.t: From μνάομαι (mnáomai, “to be mindful of, remember”) + -μη (-mē).

2163.t: Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mergʰ- (“to moisten, wet”) via a metathesized schwebeablaut form of *mregʰ- or zero-grade form *mr̥gʰ-; cognates include Latvian merguot (“to rain slowly”), merga (“soft rain”).

2164.t: Seemingly imitative of croaking, with original form something like *βρατ-αχ- (*brat-akh-), but this imitation was probably not formed in Greek, but borrowed from Pre-Greek or Semitic; compare Hebrew צְפַרְדֵּעַ (ṣəp̄ardḗaʿ), Arabic ضَفْدَع (ḍafdaʕ),…

2168.t: Morphologically from δια- (dia-) + στῆναι (stênai) + -μα (-ma), from ἵστημι (hístēmi).

2117.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tségʷomai, from Proto-Indo-European *tyegʷ- (“avoid, yield to”).

2127.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰúyō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuHyéti, from *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).

2146.t: * Masculine from Proto-Hellenic *hwādús, from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus. * Feminine from Proto-Hellenic *hwādéyya, from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂déwih₂: see -ια (-ia). Both forms are regardless from *sweh₂d- (“to be sweet”).

2129.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰolā́, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰolh₃-éh₂, from *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”).

2150.t: From Proto-Hellenic *opʰél͏̌l͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃bʰélyeti, from *h₃bʰel- (whence ὄφελος (óphelos, “benefit”)).

2162.t: From βόσκω (bóskō, “to feed, tend”) + -άνη (-ắnē, instrument noun suffix).

2144.t: From ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bring, bear, carry”).

2124.t: From τιτρώσκω (titrṓskō, “to wound”) + -μα (-mă, suffix forming neuter nouns).

2115.t: Abstract noun from σύμμαχος (súmmakhos, “fighting together”) + -ία (-íā, abstract noun suffix).

2176.t: From μνήμη (mnḗmē, “memory”) + -εῖον (-eîon), from μνάομαι (mnắomai, “I am mindful of”) + -μη (-mē).

2185.t: From πληρόω (plēróō, “to fill”) + -μα (-mă, result noun suffix).

2183.t: From παρακαλέω (părăkăléō, “to summon, encourage”) (from παρά (părắ, “near”) + καλέω (kăléō, “to call”)) + -σις (-sĭs).

2132.t: The first element is ἄκρος (ắkros, “topmost; outermost”). The second element is uncertain; it was traditionally thought to be βύω (bŭ́ō, “to stuff; to plug”), but this is almost certainly incorrect.

2199.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷʰtʰéřřō, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰér-ye-ti, from *dʰgʷʰer- (“flow, diverge; perish”) via the middle form φθείρομαι (phtheíromai, “to be destroyed, perish”) with new active meaning “destroy”.

2187.t: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *p(y)eh₂w- (“to strike, hit”), and cognate with Latin paviō (“to beat, strike”) and Lithuanian pjáuti (“to reap, cut”).

2153.t: Contraction of ὑπερώϊος (hŭperṓĭ̈os), from ὑπέρ (hŭpér, “above; over”).

2170.t: From Proto-Indo-European *denḱ- (“to bite”). Cognate with Sanskrit दशति (daśati, “to bite”), Old English ġetingan (“to press upon”), and Albanian darë.

2181.t: There are no obvious cognates. If connected with Latin natis (“rump”), it can be either assumed a derivation from an old Proto-Indo-European root noun *n(e)h₃t- or a root *nh₂t-, which became thematicized in Greek.

2155.t: From ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”) + -η (-ē), possibly inherited from Proto-Hellenic *hrowā́, from Proto-Indo-European *srowéh₂, from the root *srew- (“to flow, stream”).

2118.t: A Semitic loanword, found as Aramaic סָסָא / ܣܳܣܳܐ (sāsā, “moth”), Hebrew סָס (sās, “moth”), Akkadian 𒌨𒈨 (sāsum, “moth”), Arabic سُوس (sūs, “moth-worm”).

2145.t: From ἔδω (édō, “to eat”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

2191.t: From στάξ (stắx, “drop”) + *-ϳω (*-jō), of uncertain origin; also found in σταγών (stăgṓn, “drop”).

2131.t: The formation is similar to κάμαξ (kắmăx, “vine pole; prop”) and πίναξ (pĭ́năx, “board; plank”), and the traditional connection with Lithuanian žer̃ti (“to scrape”) does not explain the Greek formation.

2147.t: Beekes suggests an equivalence with Latin vallus (“stake; pole”) on the basis of the Aeolic variant ϝάλλος (wắllos), in which case from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn”).

2182.t: From οἶκος (oîkos, “house, home, estate”) + νόμος (nómos, “law, rule, authority”), equivalent to οἶκος (oîkos) + νέμω (némō) + -ος (-os).

2175.t: By surface analysis, λούω (loúō, “to wash, bathe”) + -τήρ (-tḗr). Compare λουτρόν (loutrón, “bathing-place”).

2130.t: From χρίω (khríō, “to rub, smear, anoint”) + -σις (-sis), forming an action noun.
